01 / THE PROBLEM

The back office is the last big function still run by hand.

Every money workflow in finance has the same three traits. Together they defeated RPA, and they are why generic agents stall here.

01

The rules are fixed

Match the invoice, find the code, gather the proof, file, post. Same steps every time. This is not a judgment problem.

02

The systems keep changing

Retailer portals, distributor sites, bank feeds and ERPs change forms, fields and logins without notice. Every hand-built integration breaks.

03

The proof arrives late

Nothing confirms success at the moment of action. The answer shows up weeks later as cash on a remittance, a denial, or silence.

Why the two existing answers failed

ApproachWhat it got rightWhere it breaks
RPA and scrapersDeterministic. Cheap per run.A portal changes a field and an engineer rebuilds the bot. Maintenance eats the budget.
Managed services with humans in the loopHandles change and judgment. Works for large accounts.Humans are the verifier, so cost scales with volume and the humans never come out.
02 / THE THESIS

Coding agents matured first because code has a verifier. Accounting has one too.

Double-entry and reconciliation check every action against cash. That is what lets a harness run finance workflows with almost no one watching.

The scaffolding layer for computer-use agents is widely described as an unsolved infrastructure problem. We build it for one function, where the verifier already exists.

03 / THE SPEC

Every money workflow is the same five-part spec.

The harness runs the spec. The customer's ERP, payers and reason codes are configuration. Deductions is the first spec; the next ones fill the same five slots.

  1. 1Obligation

    What the ledger says is owed or expected

  2. 2Evidence

    The documents that prove it

  3. 3Action

    A step taken in an outside system

  4. 4Settlement

    The real-world outcome, observed later

  5. 5Entry

    The journal entry, and the reconciliation that proves it

WorkflowObligationEvidenceActionSettlementEntry
Deductions (now)Short pay on a retailer remittanceInvoice, bill of lading, promo contract, portal claim detailFile the dispute on the retailer or distributor portalRepayment, denial or silence, weeks laterClear the deduction, book the recovery, reconcile to cash
Cash application (next)Open invoice in ARRemittance advice, bank lineApply payment in the bank portal and ARBank matchApply cash, close the invoice, reconcile the bank
Vendor chargebacks and bills (then)Vendor bill or compliance feePO, receiving record, contract termsDispute or approve on the vendor portalCredit memo or paymentBook the credit, reconcile AP

Operating rule inside every spec: code moves the money, the model only repairs a step when a system changes and reads messy documents, and the browser layer is bought from whoever wins it, not built.

04 / THE HARNESS

Accounting already solved memory, trust and failure.

These are the open problems for long-running agents. Finance has had answers for a century. We use them, and we publish three numbers to prove it.

01

Memory is the audit trail

The agent's memory is the case file and the ledger, not a vector store. Periods close and lock, so nothing compounds across them.

Clean-book rate

Share of recovery entries the accountant accepts unedited at month-end

02

Trust is a track record per step

Each step, per payer, earns its way out of human review. The gate on "file the dispute" comes off after N clean reconciliations, not on a feeling.

Unattended rate

Share of items from intake to booked recovery with zero human touches

03

Failure is caught by the books

A wrong action shows up as an entry that doesn't tie. The reconciliation catches it, not the agent's own judgment. When a portal changes, the model repairs the step and re-caches it.

Time to repair

Hours from a portal change to the workflow running again, without an engineer

All three numbers are instrumented from the first live workflow and reported per customer, per week. We would rather show a low number that climbs than a claim.

05 / THE WEDGE

Deductions is workflow one, and the hardest test.

Retailers short-pay brands, lean teams can't fight back, and the proof is pure cash. Every trait of the back office shows up here at full strength.

Up to 10%

of revenue lost to deductions at food and consumer brands. $300K to $1M a year for a $10M brand.

15 to 20

retailer and distributor portals a typical AR team logs into.

2 to 5 people

is often the whole finance team. They set a dollar threshold and eat everything below it.

Why this workflow first

Dozens of portals that change, rules that differ per retailer, and a result that only appears weeks later on a remittance. If the harness runs unattended here, cash application and payables are easier, not harder. And the value is cash, so nobody argues about the baseline.

What a $1,500 shortfall looks like to finance

InvoicePaymentShortfallReason on the remittance
$50,000$48,500$1,500A shortage code, a promo allowance and a compliance fee. Each needs different evidence.

Deduction-rate estimates are industry-published and vary widely; the shortfall example is illustrative. Initial focus is $10M to $100M brands on QuickBooks.

08 / THE ROADMAP

Deductions is the wedge. Each spec unlocks the next.

Every workflow fills the same five slots. The harness and the payer connectors are reused; only the spec changes. Each stage is unlocked by the numbers from the one before.

NOW

Deductions

Find, dispute and collect short payments, then book the accounting behind them. Chargebacks, shortages and promo claims across retailers and distributors.

Gate: live now
NEXT

Receivables

Cash application, reconciliation and collections for the same finance team. Same ledger, same payer connectors, new spec.

Gate: unlocks at 70%+ unattended on deductions
THEN

The back office

Vendor chargebacks, payables and close support. Each ERP connector, payer spec and trust record is reused for the next customer and the next workflow.

Gate: unlocks when workflow two repeats the pattern
